---
title: "Is vision zero making Montgomery County safer for people walking and biking?"

---
#Running the tests for the most recent hw "Trials, Errors and Lessons" starts on line 100

#Tests I can use

**Correlation**  I’ll look at road-level total crashes vs. serious crashes with a labeled scatterplot. If I join the drivers table, I can also compare speed limit with serious-crash share, since speed might be what really explains the state road pattern.

**Trend analysis** There's almost no before period to measure since the data starts in 2015 and Vision Zero was adopted in 2016. Instead, I can calculate rates using county population figures. I can then use those rather than raw figures.

**Z-scores** I will flag unusual months and roads with z-scores above 2, and count crashes by day of week. I’ll check that the data is roughly normal first, because road counts will probably be skewed.



# The idea

**Question:** Are crashes involving pedestrians and cyclists in Montgomery County getting more frequent or more severe, even with vision zero, and where are they happening?

**Hypothesis:** Despite the county's Vision Zero pledge (adopted in 2016, with a goal of zero traffic deaths and serious injuries by the end of 2030), crashes that seriously injure or kill pedestrians and cyclists have not significantly declined since 2015. Those crashes are concentrated on a small number of state-controlled roads (like Georgia Ave, New Hampshire Ave, Veirs Mill Rd and University Blvd), which the county doesn't control.

**Possible bump/twist:** Since Jan. 1, 2024, Maryland's crash reporting system has coded electric and non-electric scooter riders and electric cyclists as their own non-motorist types. I am curious to if those crashes involve e-scooters and e-bikes and whether they look different from other crashes.

**Why it's newsworthy:** Montgomery County has spent years and a lot of money on vision zero, but it's still unclear whether it's actually making streets safer for people walking and biking. The county says serious and fatal crashes are down compared to its 2012-2016 baseline, while news coverage (The Banner, WJLA) says traffic deaths have barely changed since 2018.

# The data

My main sources are three linked datasets from dataMontgomery

Crash reporting, non-motorists: "https://data.montgomerycountymd.gov/Public-Safety/Crash-Reporting-Non-Motorists-Data/n7fk-dce5/about_data" 
Crash reporting: "https://data.montgomerycountymd.gov/Public-Safety/Crash-Reporting-Incidents-Data/bhju-22kf/about_data"
Crash reporting, drivers: "https://data.montgomerycountymd.gov/Public-Safety/Crash-Reporting-Drivers-Data/mmzv-x632/about_data"

Documentation and related sources:

- Data.gov catalog entry for the non-motorist data: "https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/crash-reporting-non-motorists-data"
- Data.gov catalog entry for the drivers data: https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/crash-reporting-drivers-data
- Montgomery County vision zero page and annual reports "https://montgomerycountymd.gov/visionzero"
- Vision zero monthly crash data update, March 2026 (explains that scooters became their own category in 2024): "https://assets.montgomerycountymd.gov/files/2026-04/Vision_Zero_Crash_Data.pdf"


# Load libraries

```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(lubridate)
```

# Loading the data from the web

```{r load-data}
nonmotorists_url <- "https://data.montgomerycountymd.gov/api/views/n7fk-dce5/rows.csv?accessType=DOWNLOAD"
incidents_url    <- "https://data.montgomerycountymd.gov/api/views/bhju-22kf/rows.csv?accessType=DOWNLOAD"

nonmotorists <- read_csv(nonmotorists_url, guess_max = 10000) |> clean_names()
incidents    <- read_csv(incidents_url, guess_max = 10000) |> clean_names()
```


```{r dims}
n_distinct(nonmotorists$report_number)
```


# Fix the dates and figure out the time period

The date/time column comes in as text. I parse it with lubridate. I list a couple of formats because the downloaded CSV uses a format like "11/04/2026 03:38:00 PM" while the API version uses ISO dates.

```{r dates}
nonmotorists <- nonmotorists |>
  mutate(
    crash_datetime = parse_date_time(crash_date_time, orders = c("mdy IMS p", "mdy HMS", "ymd HMS", "ymd_HMS")),
    crash_date = as_date(crash_datetime),
    year = year(crash_date),
    month = floor_date(crash_date, "month")
  )

# Did any dates fail to parse?
nonmotorists |> filter(is.na(crash_datetime)) |> nrow()

# What time period does the data cover?
range(nonmotorists$crash_date, na.rm = TRUE)
```

```{r rows-by-year}
nonmotorists |>
  count(year) |>
  arrange(year)
```

```{r}
nonmotorists <- nonmotorists |>

    crash_datetime = parse_date_time(crash_date_time, orders = c("mdy IMS p", "mdy HMS", "ymd HMS")),
    crash_date = as_date(crash_datetime),

nonmotorists |> count(injury_severity)

nonmotorists <- nonmotorists |>

nonmotorists |> count(serious)
```

# Test 1: correlation (used HW12 and HW15 as main reference) 

```{r}
roads <- nonmotorists |>
  filter(!is.na(road_name)) |>
  group_by(road_name) |>
  summarize(
    total = n(),
    serious = sum(serious)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total))

roads

```
```{r}
roads |> summarize(correlation = cor(total, serious, method="pearson"))
```
```{r}
big_roads <- roads |> filter(total >= 50)

big_roads |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = total, y = serious)) +
  geom_text(aes(x = total, y = serious, label = road_name), size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(aes(x = total, y = serious), method = "lm") +
  labs(title = "Roads with the most pedestrian and cyclist crashes",
       x = "People hit, 2015-2025",
       y = "Serious or fatal injuries")
```
## Thoughts after Test 1:
I removed crashes with N/A (1,671) because it was skewing the correlation. Without it, the correlation is .94. Georgia Ave, New Hampshire Ave, Veirs Mill Rd and University Blvd, all state roads named in my hypothesis, have the most serious injuries. They also have a higher share of serious injuries (19%–28%) than the countywide average of 13%.

# Test 2: Trend analysis with rates (used CrimeRates and HW11 as main reference)

```{r}
yearly <- nonmotorists |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarize(
    total = n(),
    serious = sum(serious)
  )

yearly
```
```{r}
yearly <- yearly |>
  mutate(
    population = c(1033370, 1039327, 1047239, 1048794, 1051129, 1060926,
                   1055869, 1058546, 1064369, 1073045, 1074582),
    serious_rate = (serious / population) * 100000
  )

yearly
```
```{r}
yearly |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(x = year, y = serious_rate)) +
  geom_point(aes(x = year, y = serious_rate)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2018, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2022, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Serious pedestrian and cyclist injuries per 100,000 residents",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Rate per 100,000")
```
## Thoughts after Test 2:
The serious injury rate has not declined under Vision Zero. It averaged 8.2 per 100,000 residents in 2015–2017 and 8.7 in 2022–2025. The highest was 2022, the first year of the Vision Zero 2030 plan. The only drop came in 2020–2021, during COVID, and didn't last. This supports my hypothesis.


#Test 3: Z-score (used CarTheftZScores and HW7 as main reference)

```{r}
monthly <- nonmotorists |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarize(serious = sum(serious))

monthly |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = serious), binwidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Serious injuries per month",
       x = "Serious injuries",
       y = "Number of months")
```
```{r}
monthly <- monthly |>
  mutate(
    mean_serious = mean(serious),
    sd_serious = sd(serious),
    z_score = (serious - mean_serious) / sd_serious
  )

monthly |>
  filter(abs(z_score) > 2) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(z_score)))
```
```{r}
roads <- roads |>
  mutate(
    mean_serious = mean(serious),
    sd_serious = sd(serious),
    z_score = (serious - mean_serious) / sd_serious
  )

roads |>
  filter(z_score > 2) |>
  arrange(desc(z_score))
```
```{r}
nonmotorists |>
  mutate(day_of_week = wday(crash_date, label = TRUE)) |>
  count(day_of_week)
```

## Thoughts after Test 2:
Monthly serious injuries are normally distributed, with about 7 a month. Oct 2024 is an outlier of 20 and z-score of 4.28. Two of the three highest months fell in October and November, probably because it gets dark earlier. The two lowest months were during COVID. Crashes happen far more often on weekdays than on weekends, which can mean commuting traffic plays a role.

##Conclusion from testing:
Even with Vision Zero, people walking and biking in Montgomery County are still getting hurt or killed at about the same rate as before, and its mainly clustered in big roads like Georgia Ave, New Hampshire Ave, Veirs Mill Rd and University Blvd.
